summary: This unit teaches you to clean and prepare the offices and meeting rooms of a hotel, villa company or guest house: get in and out safely and securely, protect confidential information, clean desks, equipment, floors and glass, deal with waste, keep the staff kitchenette hygienic, restock supplies and set up and reset a meeting room.

blocks.p: Behind every hotel or villa company there are offices: reception and accounts, the manager's office, the booking desk, the staff kitchenette and the meeting room. They must be clean, tidy and ready when staff arrive, but they are also full of **private papers, computers and money**. An office cleaner works mostly out of sight, so the property must be able to trust you. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.

Cleaning an office is different from cleaning a guest room. The surfaces are desks, screens and phones, not beds and bathrooms. You must not move papers, switch off machines or read what you see. That is why this unit is about **security, confidentiality and care of equipment** as much as it is about cleaning.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the office
rows: Work safely
Prevent slips, trips, shocks, strain and chemical injuries
Report cables, leaks and faults
Keep offices secure and information private
Sign for and look after keys
Never let strangers in
Treat everything you see as confidential
Plan and prepare the work
Use a schedule and checklist
Choose the right equipment, cloths and cleaners
Clean at the right time and make sure nobody is working there
Clean the office
Dust, clean desks, equipment, glass, doors and chairs
Vacuum or mop floors
Empty bins and clean touch points
Deal with waste
Separate general waste, recycling, confidential waste and special waste
Clean the staff kitchenette and restock
Clean the sink, fridge, kettle and microwave safely
Restock soap, paper towels, water and cups
Set up and reset meeting rooms
Know the layouts and the seating
Set tables, chairs, glasses, notepads and equipment
Clear and reset after the meeting and hand in left items
Finish and report
Check the work, close windows, lock up and return the key
Fill in the record sheet and report faults

flow: Plan and collect the key
Check the office is free and enter
Prepare equipment and chemicals
Clean from high to low and from back to front
Deal with waste and the kitchenette
Restock and set up meeting rooms
Check, lock up and return the key
Record and report

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in a Centre office and meeting room. The assessor watches how you plan, enter, clean, protect confidential material and finish, not only whether the room looks clean.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: If you photograph your practical work, photograph surfaces and set-ups only. Never photograph papers, computer screens or names on documents.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Hazard
Risk
How you prevent it
rows: Cables across the floor
Trips and falls; damage to equipment
Do not move, pull, tape or unplug cables yourself
Report them so they can be moved or covered safely
Overloaded sockets and power strips
Overheating; fire
Do not plug your vacuum into an already crowded power strip
Report any socket that is hot, burnt or loose
Liquids near electrical equipment
Electric shock; damage
Never spray cleaner onto computers, phones or sockets: spray the cloth, wipe, and keep it nearly dry
Unplug a kettle or microwave before cleaning it
Wet floors
Slips
Put out a wet floor sign when you mop
Dry the floor or mop one half at a time
Lifting boxes of paper and furniture
Back strain
Use a trolley, or bend your knees and hold the load close
Ask for help with heavy items
Chemicals
Skin and eye burns; fumes
Read the label and the safety data sheet (SDS)
Wear gloves
Never mix products, such as bleach with other cleaners
Reaching to high places
Falls
Use a proper step stool or ladder, never a chair
Do not climb alone on a ladder
Shredders and printers
Fingers pulled in; hot parts
Switch off and unplug a shredder before you empty its bin
Do not push paper in by hand
Broken glass and sharp objects in bins
Cuts
Wear gloves; never push your hand into a bin; report and put sharps in a safe container

blocks.note: If you find an electrical fault, such as a burning smell, sparks or a hot plug, **leave it alone, keep people away and report it at once**. Do not touch it with wet hands or try to repair it.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Jamaica uses 110 V (and 220 V for some equipment) at 50 Hz. Water and power cuts are common in some places: ask your supervisor what to do when the lights go off, and never use candles near papers.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Product or tool
Use
Take care
rows: Neutral cleaner (pH about 7)
Everyday cleaning of laminated desks, chair mats, doors, hard floors
Mild and safe for most surfaces; dilute as the label says
Glass cleaner
Glass partitions, doors, windows
Spray onto the cloth, not the glass, near electronics
Disinfectant
Touch points, kitchenette surfaces, handsets
Clean first; leave it wet for the contact time on the label
Microfibre cloth
Dusting and wiping; picks up dust, does not leave lint
Wash after use; do not use fabric softener on them
Vacuum cleaner
Carpets and hard floors
Check the cable and filter; empty the bag or bin
Mop and bucket
Hard floors
Wring well
Use a wet floor sign
Caddy
Carries your cloths, cleaners and gloves
Keep it with you, closed and labelled

ul: Use **colour-coded cloths** so germs are not carried from dirty to clean areas. A common code is red for toilets, yellow for washrooms, blue for general areas and glass, and green for kitchens, but follow the property's own code.
Keep chemicals in their own labelled containers. Never put them on a desk, near staff cups or in the office fridge.
Wear gloves for chemicals and for bins.

blocks.p: An office holds information that could harm a guest, a worker or the property if it got into the wrong hands: guest names and passport numbers, pay records, contracts, bank details and keys to safes. You may see these things every day. You must **never read them, copy them, move them or talk about them**.

head: Rule
Why
rows: Sign out each key from the key log and sign it back in
So the property always knows who holds each key and when.
Never borrow, lend or copy a key
A key in the wrong hands is a security risk, and you are responsible for it.
Do not ask someone else to open a locked office for you
Only the person who has signed for the key is allowed in.
Never enter by a window or by any other way than the door
It is unsafe and counts as a break-in.
Never hide a key under a mat or in a plant pot
Anyone could find it.
If you lose a key, report it at once
Locks may have to be changed.

blocks.h: Visitors and people you do not know

ul: If a person you do not know asks to be let into an office, **politely refuse** and call security or a manager. This is true even if they say they are staff or a guest, and even if they say they will only be a minute.
Never let a person into an office and wait with them, and never lend them your key.
If you find a door or window open or a lock broken, do not go in. Report it to your supervisor or security at once.

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Papers on a desk
Do not read, move or tidy them into a pile. Dust and wipe round them.
A computer left on
Leave it on. Do not touch the keys, mouse or screen; clean around it.
A screen showing information
Do not read it; do not photograph it.
A document in the bin that looks private
Do not read it. Put it with confidential waste, as the rules say.
The phone rings
Let it ring, or take a message only if that is your property's rule. Never give out information.
An open drawer or safe
Do not touch the contents. Close the door only if the rules say, and report it.
Something you see or hear that worries you
Tell your supervisor. Do not tell co-workers or friends.

blocks.note: Jamaica's law on data protection says that personal information must be kept private and secure. A cleaner who talks about what is in an office could cause harm to a guest or a worker and could lose their job and be taken to court. Your discretion is part of the job.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.note: Valuable items left lying about, such as cash, a phone or a laptop, are not yours to move. Report them to your supervisor and record what you saw, so you cannot be blamed if something is missing.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Offices are usually cleaned **before or after office hours**, following the cleaning schedule, so staff are not disturbed.
If you must clean when someone is working, check first that they agree, and work quietly around them.
Use a **checklist** for each office so no task is missed and your supervisor can check it.
Gather the equipment before you start: dusters or microfibre cloths, cleaners, a vacuum, a mop and bucket, bin liners, gloves, a wet floor sign and your caddy.

flow: Check the office is free and put out signs if needed
Open the blinds or windows if the rules allow, and put on gloves
Collect rubbish and empty the bins
Dust from high to low and from back to front
Clean desks, equipment and touch points
Clean glass and doors
Clean chair mats and furniture
Vacuum or mop the floor, finishing at the door
Tidy, check, close windows, switch off lights and lock up

blocks.p: **Dust first, floors last**, because dust falls down. Work **from the back of the room towards the door**, so that you do not walk over a finished area. **Dry cleaning comes before wet cleaning**.

ul: A desk covered with papers is **not tidied**. Leave the papers where they are and clean the clear areas.
Wipe a laminated desk with a damp cloth and neutral cleaner, then dry it. Do not use bleach, scouring powder or a lot of wax.

Wipe chair arms, backs and the **chair mat** (the plastic sheet under a desk chair) with a damp cloth and neutral cleaner, and dry it. Do not use scouring powder, which makes it cloudy, or floor wax, which makes it slippery.
At the end, push chairs in neatly so that the walkways are clear and the room looks tidy.
Clear cups and plates left on desks to the kitchenette as the rules say. Do not drink or eat anything left behind.

head: Equipment
How to clean it
rows: Computer screen
A soft, dry or slightly damp microfibre cloth or a screen wipe. No bleach, no scouring pad, no glass cleaner sprayed onto it. Follow the maker's instructions.
Keyboard and mouse
Wipe the surface with a cloth slightly damp with disinfectant or a keyboard wipe. Never spray liquid onto it; liquid inside can damage it.
Telephone handset
Wipe with a disinfectant wipe or a cloth damp with disinfectant. It is touched all day and spreads germs.
Printer and photocopier
Wipe the outside with a dry or barely damp cloth. Do not open the machine or touch the glass unless that is your task. Load paper only if it is part of your job.
Power strips, sockets and cables
Dust the outside with a dry cloth; never use liquid near them; report any damage.
Shredder
Switch off and unplug before you empty the bin. Never push paper in by hand.

blocks.note: Never spray cleaner **straight onto** a keyboard, phone or screen: the liquid can get inside, damage it and cause a shock. Spray the cloth, wipe, and let the surface dry.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Clean and disinfect the things people touch most: door handles, light switches, phone handsets, keyboards, mouse, desk edges, chair arms, tap handles and the fridge and microwave door handles. Use a cloth damp (not dripping) with disinfectant and let it stay wet for the contact time on the label.

ul: For a glass partition or door, **spray glass cleaner onto a cloth** and wipe from the top downwards. Finish with a dry cloth.
Never use the cloth from bin lids or the toilet. Use the cloth for glass only.
Wipe fingermarks from door frames and push plates.

head: Floor
Method
rows: Carpet
Pull out chairs and move small items, vacuum under desks and chairs, then put everything back. Vacuum in slow, overlapping passes. Report stains for special treatment.
Hard floors (tiles, vinyl, wood)
Dust-mop or vacuum first, then damp-mop with neutral cleaner. Wring the mop well and put out a wet floor sign. Use as little water as possible on wood.
Edges and corners
Use the crevice tool; do not leave them out.

ul: Check the vacuum cable and plug before use. Keep the cable behind you and away from the nozzle.
Never push desks against a wall or move computers. If something must be moved, ask the staff or put it back exactly as it was.

blocks.p: An office makes several kinds of waste. Mixing them wastes money, puts private papers at risk and can hurt a person. Sort waste as the property's system says.

head: Kind of waste
Examples
What to do
rows: Confidential waste
Papers with names, pay, guest details, bank details
Put in the locked bin or bag for shredding. Never read it, never put it in the ordinary bin and never take it home.
Paper recycling
Clean scrap paper, envelopes, packaging card that is not confidential
Put in the recycling bin.
Plastic, cans and bottles
Empty drink bottles and cans
Rinse if needed and put in the recycling bin.
General waste
Food waste, used cups, greasy paper plates, tissues
Bag it, tie it and take it to the waste area. Do not put food in with paper recycling.
Special waste (e-waste, batteries, ink cartridges, light bulbs)
Used printer cartridges, batteries, broken tubes and bulbs
Put aside for special waste or recycling. Never burn them, never put them in the ordinary or paper bins and never pour ink down the sink.
Sharps and broken glass
Broken glass, blades, pins
Wrap or box it safely and label it. Wear gloves.

ul: Wear gloves when you empty bins. Hold the bag away from your body and never push down the contents with your hand.
Replace the bin liner, and wipe the bin if it is dirty.
Report anything unusual in a bin, such as cash, a laptop or a document that looks important, rather than throwing it away.
Used batteries and ink cartridges contain harmful materials. Keep them for the property's special collection.

blocks.note: Never burn waste, such as paper, plastic or batteries, behind the building. It makes smoke, is unsafe and damages the environment. Jamaica's waste agencies run schemes for plastics and e-waste, and your property may use them.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Put on gloves and put out a wet floor sign
Clear used cups and plates and wash or stack them as the rules say
Wipe worktops and the outside of cupboards with neutral cleaner, then disinfect
Clean the sink and taps with the cloth for that area, and dry them
Unplug the kettle and microwave, then wipe them inside and out and descale the kettle as the rules say
Check and clean the fridge
Empty the bin and replace the liner
Mop the floor and leave the sign until it is dry
Restock soap, paper towels, tea supplies and water

ul: A food fridge should be kept at **5 °C or below**. Many properties aim for about 3 to 5 °C. Follow the property's food safety rules.
Remove food that is out of date, mouldy or has been there too long, **as the property's rules say**, which may mean telling the owner or putting a notice up first.
Wipe the shelves and door seals with a cloth damp with mild cleaner, and dry them.
A fridge that is warm, leaking or smells should be reported. Do not switch it off with food inside, and do not leave the door open.

blocks.note: Always **unplug a kettle or microwave before you clean it**, and make sure your hands are dry. Water and electricity cause shocks.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Supply
What you check
rows: Hand soap and paper towels
Dispensers are full, working and clean.
Drinking water and cups
Water jugs or coolers are full; cups are clean and stocked.
Tea, coffee, sugar (if the property provides them)
Containers topped up and tidy.
Bin liners and cleaning supplies
Enough for the next shift.
Printer and copier paper
Refilled only if that is your task; load as the guide shows, not bent or crammed.
Stationery
Only restock what you have been told to; do not open cash boxes or private drawers.

ul: Report low stock to your supervisor in good time. Use the oldest stock first.
Never take supplies home, and do not use office supplies for your own use.
Water plants only as the care plan says, not every hour. Wipe dusty leaves with a damp cloth. Do not use furniture polish on leaves.
Report a leak, a dripping air-conditioner or a broken window lock at once, and protect desks and papers if it is safe to do so.

blocks.p: A meeting room must be clean, comfortable and set exactly as the booking says. Check the booking: the number of people, the layout, the equipment, the water and notepads and the start time.

head: Layout
How it looks
Good for
rows: Boardroom style
One long table with chairs round it, and usually one at each end
Small formal meetings; everyone can see and talk to each other
Theatre style
Rows of chairs facing the front, with no tables
Talks and presentations with many people
Classroom style
Rows of tables with chairs facing the front
Training; people need to write
U-shape
Tables set in a U, with chairs on the outside
Training and discussions with a presenter
Cabaret style
Round tables with chairs on part of the circle, facing the front
Group work and events

blocks.p: At a boardroom table, count the chairs on each long side and add the chairs at the ends. Example: **5 chairs on each long side and 1 at each end seat 12 people**. For a meeting of 14 people with 1 chair at each end, you need 6 chairs along each long side.

ul: Leave enough room behind each chair for people to move, and keep the **walkways and fire exits clear**.
Do not set more places than the room safely holds. Follow the room's limit.

flow: Check the booking and the layout
Clean the room and the table
Arrange the table and chairs, evenly spaced
At each place put a notepad, a pen and a water glass
Put the agenda at each seat, if provided
Set jugs of water, and a tray for used cups if needed
Check the equipment works: projector, screen, laptop connections, lights and air conditioning
Check the room temperature and the signs on the door
Do a last look for dust, marks and missing items

head: Item
Rule
rows: Glasses
Carry and set them by the base or the lower part, **never touching the rim** or putting fingers inside. They must be clean and polished.
Notepads and pens
Square to the table edge, the same at every seat; pens that work.
Agenda
A list of the topics for the meeting; place at each seat if provided.
Water jugs
Filled and placed where people can reach them.
Projector and screen
Check that it switches on and the picture is clear. Do not change settings or open files.
Air conditioning
Set the room to a comfortable temperature before people arrive; keep the room cool but not cold.

flow: Wait until the meeting has finished and the room is empty
Collect glasses, cups and plates; clear rubbish
Look for items left behind and hand them in to your supervisor or reception; record them
Wipe the table and clean spills
Reset the layout as the next booking needs
Switch off equipment as the rules say, and close the room
Report any damage or faulty equipment

ul: Do not leave used cups in a locked room.
Never take notepads, pens or items left behind for yourself. Hand in all left items; they may be important.
Wipe boards and tidy cables only as your task says.

blocks.note: Left-behind laptops, phones, folders and chargers are the owner's property. Hand them in at once, note where you found them, and do not open or look inside folders.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Walk round the room with your checklist
Check floors, desks, glass, bins and the kitchenette
Check nothing is left behind, such as cloths or chemicals
Close windows and blinds as the rules say
Switch off lights, fans and air conditioners (not computers or equipment unless told)
Close and lock the door as the property's rules say
Return the key and sign it in
Fill in the record sheet and report any faults

ul: Do not leave the door open to dry the floor or leave the lights on to make the room look busy.
Never hide a key; return it to where the rules say.
Check that your equipment and chemicals are stored away, not left in the office.

head: What to write
Example
rows: Date, time and your name
10 November, 6:30 p.m., S. Brown
Areas cleaned
Accounts office, manager's office, kitchenette
Tasks done
Dusted, vacuumed, emptied bins, restocked soap
Faults found
Air conditioner dripping in the manager's office; window lock broken
Items found
A phone left in the meeting room; handed to reception
Stock needed
Paper towels and bin liners

head: Fault
What to do
rows: Air conditioner leaking onto a desk
Protect the desk and papers if it is safe, and report straight away.
Broken window lock or door lock
Report to your supervisor or maintenance at once. Do not leave it for later.
Electrical fault, burning smell
Keep people away; report at once; do not touch it.
Broken or faulty furniture
Take it out of use if it is unsafe and report it.
Missing or damaged items
Do not move anything; report and record what you saw.

blocks.note: Do not wipe up a leak and say nothing. A small leak that is reported gets fixed; one that is hidden can ruin computers and papers.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: I can name the hazards in an office and say how to deal with each one.
I can explain why liquid must never be sprayed onto a keyboard, phone or screen.
I can sign for and look after keys, and refuse entry to a person I do not know.
I can explain why I must never read, move or talk about information in an office.
I can plan the cleaning, check that nobody is working in the office and gather the right equipment.
I can clean from high to low and back to front, and finish at the door.
I can clean desks, screens, keyboards, phones, glass and chair mats safely.
I can vacuum under desks and mop hard floors with a wet floor sign.
I can sort general, recycling, confidential and special waste.
I can clean the kitchenette and fridge, and unplug the kettle and microwave first.
I can restock soap, paper towels, water and cups and report low stock.
I can name the main meeting room layouts and work out the seating.
I can set up a boardroom meeting and check the equipment.
I can clear and reset the room and hand in left items.
I can lock up, return the key, fill in the record sheet and report faults.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I spray the cleaner onto the cloth and not onto the keyboard, because liquid can get inside and damage it or cause a shock.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Confidential
Private: must not be read, copied or talked about.
Confidential waste
Papers that must be shredded so nobody can read them.
Shredder
A machine that cuts paper into thin strips.
Key log
The book or sheet where keys are signed in and out.
Microfibre cloth
A soft cloth that picks up dust and does not leave lint.
Neutral cleaner
A mild cleaner that is safe for most surfaces.
Touch point
A surface that many people touch, such as a handle or switch.
Trip hazard
Something on the floor, such as a cable, that people could catch their foot on.
Power strip
A lead with several sockets that lets plugs share one wall socket.
Stationery
Pens, paper, envelopes and staples used in an office.
Photocopier
A machine that makes paper copies of documents.
Projector
A machine that shows a picture from a laptop on a screen or wall.
Kitchenette
A small kitchen area where staff make tea and coffee.
Boardroom style
One long table with chairs around it.
Theatre style
Rows of chairs facing the front, with no tables.
Classroom style
Rows of tables with chairs facing the front.
Agenda
The list of topics for a meeting.
Special waste
Waste such as batteries, cartridges and bulbs that needs separate disposal.
SDS
Safety data sheet, which comes with a chemical.
Wet floor sign
A sign that warns people the floor is wet.

c1.title: The locked accounts office in Montego Bay
c1.text: At 6 p.m. cleaner Shanelle goes to clean the accounts office of a Montego Bay hotel. The door is locked, and she has not signed for the key because the key log is in the supervisor's office, which is also locked. A co-worker says she has a spare key for the accounts office and offers to lend it. Inside, there are printed guest lists with passport details lying open on the desks and a computer showing a spreadsheet.

c2.title: Cleaning the head office in Kingston
c2.text: Trainee Rashad is cleaning the Kingston head office of a villa company before the staff arrive at 8 a.m. The desks are covered with papers, and on one desk a keyboard has fingermarks and crumbs on it. A power strip under the manager's desk is crowded with plugs and feels warm, and there is a long cable across the doorway. The glass partition is smeared. He has a spray bottle of glass cleaner and a microfibre cloth.

c3.title: Sorting the bins in Mandeville
c3.text: In a Mandeville property office, trainee Camille is emptying the bins. Among the contents she finds an empty printer ink cartridge, a half-eaten patty on a greasy paper plate, clean scrap paper, a page headed 'Staff salary review', two used batteries and a broken mug. The office has a general bin, a paper recycling bin, a locked confidential bag and a box for special waste.

c4.title: A board meeting at an Ocho Rios resort
c4.text: A resort in Ocho Rios has booked its boardroom for 14 people, in boardroom style, starting at 10 a.m. Trainee Orville has an hour to set up, and he works out first how the table and chairs must go. The room has one long table, 16 chairs, a projector and a jug of water. When the meeting ends at noon, he finds a laptop charger, a closed folder and some used cups on the table.

c5.title: The kitchenette in Spanish Town
c5.text: Trainee Joelle is cleaning the staff kitchenette in a Spanish Town office block. The fridge thermometer reads 9 °C, and there is a container of old rice, a half-full box of juice and a staff lunch with a name on it. The kettle is plugged in and has white scale inside. The floor has a spill by the sink.

c6.title: Locking up in Portmore
c6.text: At the end of her evening shift in a Portmore property office, cleaner Latoya notices water dripping from the air conditioner onto the manager's desk, which has papers on it. A man she has not seen before says he is the manager's friend and asks her to let him into the manager's office to collect a file. She also sees that one window lock is broken. She has finished all the cleaning.

questions.q: What should Shanelle do about the locked door?
o: Borrow her co-worker's spare key to get in
Ask security to open it with any key that fits
Wait for a staff member to sign out the key for her
Sign for her own key, or report that she cannot
questions.why: Keys are signed out by the person who will use them. If the key log or the key cannot be had, report it to the supervisor; never borrow or use an unsigned spare key.

questions.q: How should Shanelle deal with the guest lists lying open on the desks?
o: Gather them into one pile so that she can clean the desks
Leave them where they are and clean around them
Read them to check whether any guests have been missed
Put them in the drawer and lock it for safety
questions.why: Papers in an office are confidential. Do not read, move or talk about them. Clean the clear areas and report anything that worries you.

questions.q: The spreadsheet is still open on the computer. What should she do?
o: Switch the computer off so it saves power
Scroll down to see if the work has been saved
Leave it on and not touch the keys or screen
Close the spreadsheet so that nobody else can read it
questions.why: Switching off or touching a computer could lose someone's work. Leave it exactly as it is and clean around it.

questions.q: What is the best way for Rashad to clean the keyboard?
o: Spray disinfectant straight onto the keys and wipe
Tip it upside down and shake out the crumbs over the carpet
Wipe the keys with a cloth slightly damp with disinfectant
Wash it under the tap and leave it to dry on the desk
questions.why: Liquid inside a keyboard can damage it or cause a shock. Use a cloth that is barely damp, and let it dry.

questions.q: What should Rashad do about the warm, crowded power strip?
o: Report it and avoid using it, as it may be a fire risk
Unplug some of the plugs to make room for the vacuum
Cover it with a cloth so that it cannot be seen
Pour a little water on it to cool it down
questions.why: A warm, overloaded strip can overheat and cause a fire. Do not add to the load, touch it with wet hands or move the plugs; report it.

questions.q: How should he clean the smeared glass partition?
o: With the cloth from the bin lids, to save time
With a wet cloth, leaving it to dry in the air
With a dry paper towel and furniture polish
With glass cleaner on a cloth, wiping from the top down
questions.why: Spray the cleaner onto the cloth, not the glass, and wipe from the top down so drips run onto an unwiped area. Use a clean cloth kept for glass.

questions.q: Where should Camille put the page headed 'Staff salary review'?
o: In the confidential bag for shredding
In the paper recycling bin
On the manager's desk, to ask if it is needed
In the general bin, after tearing it in half
questions.why: A page with pay details is confidential. She should not read it, and it goes in the locked confidential bag, never in an ordinary bin.

questions.q: Where do the two used batteries and the ink cartridge go?
o: In the general bin with the food waste
In the box for special waste, to be recycled safely
In the paper recycling bin with the scrap paper
Down the sink, after emptying out the ink
questions.why: Batteries and cartridges contain harmful materials and need special collection. They must never be burned, poured away or mixed with other waste.

questions.q: What should Camille do with the broken mug?
o: Put it in the recycling bin with the cans and bottles
Pick up the pieces with her bare hands and put them in a bin
Wrap it safely, wearing gloves, and put it in the general waste
Leave it on the floor beside the bin, with a note
questions.why: Broken crockery is a cut hazard. Wear gloves, wrap the pieces so no one is cut and put them in the general waste; do not put them in recycling.

questions.q: Next week the resort wants a training session where 20 staff take notes while a presenter talks at the front. Which layout should Orville plan?
o: Classroom style, with rows of tables facing the front
Boardroom style, with all 20 round one long table
Theatre style, with rows of chairs and no tables
Cabaret style, with round tables for group games
questions.why: People who must write need a table, and they face the presenter, so classroom style fits. Theatre style has no tables, and boardroom and cabaret layouts seat people facing each other or in groups.

questions.q: How should Orville carry and set the water glasses?
o: Holding them by the base, never touching the rim
Stacked, one inside the other, to save trips
With his fingers inside the rim to carry more at once
By the top edge so he does not drop them
questions.why: Glasses are held by the base or the lower part. Touching the rim or inside spreads germs and leaves marks.

questions.q: Which check is most important before the meeting begins?
o: That the curtains are closed and the lights are off
That the projector and other equipment work and the seating is right
That the chairs are stacked so the room looks bigger
That the windows are open to let the cool air out
questions.why: People arrive expecting working equipment and the right seating. Test the projector, check the room temperature and make sure everything is as booked.

questions.q: What should Orville do with the laptop charger and the closed folder?
o: Open the folder to find the owner's name
Hand them in to his supervisor or reception and record them
Put them in the room's drawer for the next booking
Keep them safe at home until somebody asks
questions.why: Left items belong to someone. Hand them in at once and record where they were found, without opening or reading anything.

questions.q: What does the fridge reading of 9 °C tell Joelle?
o: It is the right temperature for food
It is too warm; it should be 5 °C or below, so she should report it
It is too cold, so she should switch it off
It does not matter, as the fridge is not for guests
questions.why: A food fridge should be at 5 °C or below. At 9 °C bacteria grow quickly, so report the fault and follow the property's food rules.

questions.q: What should Joelle do before cleaning the kettle?
o: Switch it on to loosen the scale
Unplug it, and make sure her hands are dry
Fill it with bleach to remove the scale
Wash it in the sink, with the plug in
questions.why: Always unplug an electrical appliance before cleaning it, to avoid shock. Descale as the property's rules and the maker say.

questions.q: What should she do about the old rice and the juice in the fridge?
o: Throw away everything in the fridge, including the named lunch
Share out the food to staff before it spoils
Leave it all in the fridge until the owners come back
Remove spoiled or out-of-date items, by the rules
questions.why: Old food is a food-safety risk. Remove items that are out of date or spoiled as the rules say, but do not throw out a named lunch that is still good.

questions.q: The man says he is the manager's friend. What should Latoya do?
o: Let him in, but stay with him while he looks
Let him in if he promises to be quick
Politely refuse, and call security or a manager
Lend him the key so he can lock up afterwards
questions.why: No stranger may be let into an office, whatever he says. Refuse politely and call security or a manager to deal with it.

questions.q: What should she do about the air conditioner dripping onto the manager's desk?
o: Wipe up the water and say nothing, since it will soon stop
Move the papers to the floor and put a bucket there
Switch off the power to the whole building
Protect the desk if safe, and report it at once
questions.why: A leak can ruin papers and computers. Protect what you safely can and report it so it is fixed; never ignore or hide it.

questions.q: Whom should Latoya tell about the broken window lock?
o: Her supervisor or maintenance, straight away
The first person she meets in the car park
Nobody, as windows are not her job
A friend who can mend it at the weekend
questions.why: A broken lock is a security risk. Tell the supervisor or maintenance at once and write it on the record sheet.

questions.q: Before she leaves, what is the best use of the record sheet?
o: Throw it away, since the work is done
Fill in the work done, faults and items found, then hand it in
Keep it at home in case it is needed
Leave it on a desk for the office staff to complete
questions.why: The record sheet proves the work was done and passes on faults and stock needs. Complete it and hand it in.
